chapter: Retirement and the future of big bands
title: Billy Strayhorn and the eight bars Barnet never got
summary: He remembers Strayhorn's compositions and how he repeatedly asked for just eight bars of an arrangement.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: A little earlier we were talking about
Billy Strayhorn, and I don't think we've talked about him on the tape.
What do you particularly remember about Billy Strayhorn?
Well, let's see. "Prelude to a Kiss," "Warm Valley," "Chelsea Bridge," "Passion Flower," and a lot of other beautiful things.
You were telling me that during your long friendship with Strayhorn you repeatedly asked him for just eight bars?

Oh, yeah. I kept saying to him, you know, I said, "How about writing me an arrangement?" And he would say, "No, I really can't." And I would say, "Well, look, just eight bars. How about eight bars and we'll build a whole thing on it," and I never did get the eight bars. But we used to joke about it. It became a thing. He was a fantastic man. He -- I can't think of any greater complement to Duke than his finding Billy Strayhorn, because it was such a wonderful mixture. Billy Strayhorn gave a delicacy to the Ellington band and a warmth that even exceeded Duke's efforts in those areas. And I've often wondered, as we were talking about him, between tapes, I mean, how he felt about some of the things that were credited to Duke which were really his work.
